name: Bole
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: 29. Bolenchi follows the same rules as Hausa for the inter-relation of tone and stress, i.e. stressed syllables have High Tone and unstressed syllables have Low Tone. They both employ three Falling Tones (1) High to Low. (2) Mid to below Low. (3) Low falling lower. [...] Stress is marked after the syllable; the main stress is marked with " e.g. do"ki; secondary stress is marked with ' e.g. tam"baya' (last syllable). Tones are marked below the syllable. There are three simple tones: High has no mark below the vowel [...]. Low Tone is indicated by a horizontal line below e.g. doki (High, Low). Mid Tone is marked by a small circle below e.g. kogi (Low, Mid).
new_statements.citation: Abraham, R. C. 1929. The Bolenchi [Bolanci] language and the conclusions to be drawn from it. Typescript (Kaduna Archives file K.119), 76 pp.; copy circulated by the UCLA Yobe Languages Research Project (Box). Fika variety.
new_statements.locator: §29 'Comparative Philology of the Hausa-Bolenchi-Angass group', typescript p. 114 (pdf p. 13); 'Method of Transcription', typescript p. 204 (pdf p. 21); cf. §20 p. 110 (pdf p. 10) 'the tone-stress system of Bolenchi is almost identical with Hausa' and 'Tone and Stress of the Past Tense', p. 205 (pdf p. 22).
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: In Abraham's 1929 (pre-phonemic, Hausa-modelled) analysis Bole has no stress independent of tone: a 'stressed' syllable is simply one bearing High tone and an 'unstressed' one bears Low tone, so 'stress' placement follows the lexical and grammatical tone melody of the word (e.g. Past-tense trisyllabic transitives High-Low-Mid vs intransitives Low-Mid-Low), not any positional rule. All modern descriptions (Gimba 1998, 2000; Gimba, Ali, Bah & Schuh 2009; Schuh's UCLA site) treat Bole as a two-tone (H/L) register language with downdrift, tone spreading and contrastive vowel length, and never mention stress at all.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Abraham marks a 'secondary stress' (') after the syllable, e.g. tam"baya' ('last syllable'), apparently corresponding to his Mid tone; no placement rule is given. Modern sources: none.
new_statements.exceptions: None as such; Abraham lists tone-stress patterns by verb length and transitivity in the Past tense (disyllabic intransitives High-Low; trisyllabic transitives High-Low-Mid, intransitives mostly Low-Mid-Low with a few High-High-Low; quadrisyllabic transitives usually Low-Mid-Low-Mid). Modern work (Gimba 1998, 2000; dictionary 2009) describes Low Tone Raising and 'variable tone' words (phrase-final H-L becoming H-H medially).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (verb forms and nouns in isolation), Fika variety; Abraham's 'stress' is a tone correlate, not a separately measured prominence. The authoritative modern primary description (Gimba 2000, p. 8: 'Bole is a register tone language... two level tones, high (H) and low (L)', file) is silent on stress; an instrumental study of Bole intonation (Schuh, Gimba & Ritchart 2010) exists but could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: All opened sources describe the Fika (Fikka) variety of Bole (Abraham 1929: 'the language... spoken at Fikka'; 2009 dictionary: 'based on the variety of Bole spoken in Fika'); Schuh 1983 (not opened) describes the Gadaka dialect. Glottolog nucl1695 has no separate dialect glottocodes for Fika/Bara. Abraham's 'Bolenchi/Bolanci' = Bole.

sources.citation: Gimba, Alhaji Maina. 2000. Bole verb morphology. PhD dissertation, UCLA (chair R. G. Schuh). xxiv+223 pp.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: online with a Harvard login (also: harvard online access (harvardkey))
sources.note: Ch. 2 'Tones and Tone Rules', §2.0 p. 8 (pdf p. 32): 'Bole is a register tone language whereby the pitch height of the voice from syllable to syllable is phonologically contrastive. Bole has two level tones, high (H) and low (L).' Contour tones only on monosyllables (mostly contractions); Low Tone Raising, tone of clitics. The word 'stress' does not occur anywhere in the dissertation ('accent' only for the diacritics).

sources.citation: Gimba, Alhaji Maina. 1990. A study of the Bole dialects. MA thesis, Bayero University, Kano. 90 pp.
sources.note: Ch. 2 'Sound structure of Bole' (consonants, vowels, length and tone). Scan is very light; scanned layer mostly unreadable (UCLA page itself warns of this); no 'stress' recoverable from the text layer, so effectively unknown.

sources.citation: Gimba, Alhaji Maina, Malam Baba Ali & Madu Bah; ed. Russell G. Schuh. 2009. Bole-English-Hausa Dictionary, 2nd edition. Potiskum: Ajami Press / Yobe Languages Research Project (NSF BCS-0553222). 187 pp. Fika variety.
sources.note: Introduction pp. iii-vi: 'The distinctions between long and short vowels and distinctions between tones (whether a syllable is spoken with a higher or lower voice pitch) are both important for correct pronunciation and for distinguishing the meanings of words in Bole'; marks low, falling, rising tones and vowel length; notes 'variable tone' H-L ~ H-H words. No mention of stress.

sources.citation: Gimba, Alhaji Maina. 2006. Jinsi a Bolanci ('Gender in Bole'). Studies in African Linguistics 35 (Schuh Festschrift supplement): 67-74. DOI 10.32473/sal.v35i0.107317 (in Hausa).
sources.note: Morphosyntax of gender only; nothing on prosody.

sources.citation: Schuh, Russell G. 2005. Yobe State, Nigeria as a linguistic area. Proceedings of BLS 31(2). DOI 10.3765/bls.v31i2.825 (two copies: 33-pp. author PDF from UCLA Box with text layer; 18-pp. journal scan without text layer).
sources.note: Areal survey of Bole, Karekare, Ngamo, Bade, Ngizim, Duwai: vowel systems, consonants, 'rightward tone spreading' shared by most Yobe languages. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Bole language' (accessed 2026-09-17), citing Gimba 2000 p. 223 for the inventories and Omniglot for tone.
sources.note: 'Bole has two tones, a high tone marked with an acute accent and a low tone marked with a grave accent.' Nothing on stress. Its external links point to the dead aflang.linguistics.ucla.edu host and the MPI handle 11858/00-001M-0000-0012-7677-1 (Anubis-blocked).

sources.citation: Gimba, Alhaji Maina. 1998. Low Tone Raising in Bole. MA thesis, UCLA Department of Linguistics. 65 pp.
sources.note: §1.1 Tonal Structure, p. 2: 'Bole has two level tones high and low'; rising and falling contours; tone sandhi (LTR) across prosodic phrases. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Schuh, Russell G. (site author). 'Bole' page and Yobe Languages Research Project pages, African Languages at UCLA (aflang.humanities.ucla.edu), with the full Bole bibliography and Box links.
sources.note: Overview says Bole and Hausa share 'a two-tone system with downdrift'. 'Bolanci genitives with remarks on underlying contour tones and tone sequences', Gimba 1986 BA thesis 'A contrastive analysis of English and Bole phonology'. No stress statement.
